title: Trello Slack Integration: Setup and Limits (2026)
summary: Trello Slack integration posts cards to Slack and sends notifications. It lacks custom routing, field mapping, and two-way sync features.
body_markdown:
## Trello Slack settings and limits


Before you need a workflow tool, you'll run into limits in three places: which board events can notify a channel, what your plans allow, and what Slack lets an app do per minute.


### Notification types and which events trigger them


When something happens on a board you've linked to a channel, the Trello Power-Up for Slack posts it: cards created or moved, comments, due dates, attachments. You pick the events per board-and-channel pair.


If sales cards and support cards share a board, everything lands in the same channel, and you can't route one list to a different place.


The catch is that the setting is per pair, not per list or label. That's the first sign you need a workflow tool.


### Power-Up limits by Trello plan


250 runs a month on Free and 1,000 on Standard: according to Trello, that is the ceiling on its built-in automation, and plan limits show up as ceilings on volume, which means you need to choose your tier based on your expected automation volume.


At 250 runs, one busy board with a few rules can burn the month's quota in days, and after that the rules stop firing without anyone noticing, leaving you without automation for the rest of your billing cycle.


10 apps is the cap on Slack's Free plan. Once you add Trello, a calendar, a help desk and a few others, you're deciding which app to remove before you can add the next one.


### Slack app permissions and private channels


Whether you can connect a channel at all depends on how your Slack workspace handles installs. Many workspaces require an admin to approve new apps, so the person who wants the integration often can't finish the setup alone.


Skip one step on a private channel and notifications fail with no obvious error: the app has to be invited into the channel before it can post there.


Anything custom you build inherits Slack's API rate limits, which are grouped into tiers per method. The[Slack rate-limit documentation](https://docs.slack.dev/apis/web-api/rate-limits) sets them at:


- Tier 1: 1 request per minute
- Tier 2: 20 requests per minute
- Tier 3: 50 requests per minute
- Tier 4: 100 requests per minute


A method in Tier 1 handles a trickle, so a burst of 30 card moves can't all post at once. A Tier 4 method has about a hundred times that room.


Look up the tier of the exact method your flow calls before you promise anyone real-time updates.
